Abdul El‑Sayed, a progressive, wins Michigan Senate Democratic primary in key battle for party’s future
Critical of Israel and a proponent of universal public healthcare, the contender scored a narrow victory in the swing state after an all‑night count
Abdul El-Sayed has won Michigan’s Democratic nomination for U.S. Senate, defeating U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens with 48.5% of the vote, both CNN and the Associated Press reported, calling it “a massive victory for the party’s progressive wing in a battleground state.” The close race reflects how divided the party is, as well as the rise of a leftist wing that demands change.
The 41‑year‑old physician, the son of Egyptian immigrants and a representative of the Democratic Party’s progressive wing, has landed a blow in the debate over the future of Democratic opposition to Donald Trump by defeating Haley Stevens, who had the backing of the party’s heavyweights as well as special interest groups. El-Sayed’s campaign said Stevens called to concede Wednesday, according to AP.
The vote shows that the rise of young left‑wing (and even self-styled socialist) politicians is not confined to liberal strongholds. The wave that Zohran Mamdani began last year with his win in New York has spread to a swing state like Michigan, where either Republicans or Democrats can hold sway. El‑Sayed’s victory confirms that the party of Barack Obama and Joe Biden is entering a new era in which the old rules no longer apply.
The hardest part still lies ahead for El‑Sayed. After beating the centrist Stevens, he will have to prove in November that a candidate like himself — a Muslim and a proponent of ideas that were until recently viewed as radical — can defeat the Republican candidate in the midterm elections. If he were to succeed, he would become the first Muslim senator in U.S. history and join figures such as Senator Bernie Sanders, Representative Alexandria Ocasio‑Cortez and Mayor Mamdani on the list of leaders changing the face of the Democratic Party.
El‑Sayed does not describe himself as a socialist, but he champions causes largely associated with the left. He rose to prominence in Michigan on platforms such as ending unconditional U.S. aid to Israel — which he accuses openly of genocide in Gaza — and advancing universal public healthcare. He combines that message with a personal magnetism, and is often seen wearing a fitted black T‑shirt in videos that show him lifting weights in a gym or dancing in a cowboy hat to Taylor Swift’s You

corpus.title: Israel critic wins US Senate primary despite record AIPAC spending on rival (VIDEOS)

Israel critic wins US Senate primary despite record AIPAC spending on rival (VIDEOS)
Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive and staunch critic of Israel’s wars in the Middle East, has narrowly won Michigan’s Democratic US Senate primary despite record spending by the pro-Israel lobbying group AIPAC in support of his rival.
El-Sayed, the son of Egyptian immigrants and a former health official who has never held elected office, received 48.48% of the vote on Tuesday, according to the AP. His main opponent, moderate US Representative Haley Stevens, received 47.51%. El-Sayed would become the first Muslim US senator if he defeats former Republican Congressman Mike Rogers in November.
Throughout his campaign, El-Sayed has repeatedly described Israel’s war in Gaza as a “genocide” and argued that the Israeli government was as “bloodthirsty” and as “evil” as Hamas. He said he opposed “unconditional” military aid to any country, including Israel.
“I don’t want to fund a foreign military that does genocide, apartheid, or is taking us to a war we don’t need to fight. I believe in equal rights to peace, dignity and self-determination for Jewish-Israelis and Palestinians alike,” the Democrat told CNN.
The American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) spent $32 million helping Stevens, an amount the AP described as the group’s largest-ever investment in a single race.
According to the New York Times, AIPAC funding accounted for more than half of the money spent by dozens of outside groups on advertising supporting Stevens.
Several Jewish organizations have denounced El-Sayed’s stance, including the Jewish Democratic Council of America (JDCA). The American Jewish Committee (AJC) described his victory as “a deeply troubling reflection of the growing mainstreaming of divisive rhetoric and exclusionary politics in America.”
Speaking in Las Vegas on Wednesday, US President Donald Trump said El-Sayed was “full of s**t” and a “man of hate.”
“He doesn’t love Jewish people. He hates them with a passion that burns in his heart,” Trump said.

corpus.title: There’s No Time for Centrists to Be Doomers About El-Sayed’s Victory
corpus.signal_text:
Eoin Higgins is the author of “Owned: How Tech Billionaires on the Right Bought the Loudest Voice on the Left.”
Abdul El-Sayed is the Democratic Party’s nominee for the Senate in Michigan after besting Rep. Haley Stevens by less than 1 percentage point. Not long after The Associated Press called the race on Wednesday morning, Stevens threw her “full support” behind El-Sayed. While the votes were still being counted on Tuesday night, state Sen. Mallory McMorrow — who had dropped out of the running in July — also endorsed her former opponent, acknowledging that despite a “brutal” primary race, what is most important now is to head into November as a “unified party.”
What remains to be seen is whether moderates and Democratic Party pundits will follow suit, get on board, and vote blue no matter who.
But centrists seem more interested in saving face than a Senate majority. Complaining that primary voters picked the candidate more likely to lose on Election Day has become a face-saving tactic for moderates as they’ve watched their preferred picks lose against upstart insurgent campaigns like El-Sayed’s.
Among them are The Atlantic’s Jon Chait, who’s never met a progressive candidate he won’t sneer at. In typical form, Chait concern-trolled last weekend over the potential that Democrats would lose Michigan’s Senate seat by picking the charismatic El-Sayed over Stevens.
“Is there a single el-Sayed supporter with enough self-awareness to admit they’re willing to accept a higher risk of defeat to elect a left-wing candidate?” Chait asked on X, citing polling showing Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers with a slight but consistent lead in the Senate race just outside the margin of error
A more honest commentator might have pointed out that El-Sayed beat back an establishment campaign with tens of millions of dollars behind it: a staggering $62 million poured into the state to boost Stevens, half of it from AIPAC, giving her and her allies a 9-to-1 spending advantage over El-Sayed. But honesty has seldom been important for Chait’s left-bashing.
By Wednesday morning, Chait had once again reframed the race, this time as a key battle in an existential war for liberalism. He groused variously about the streamer Hasan Piker, who campaigned for El-Sayed; democratic socialism; and James Carville.
